label: Catastrophic risk: the future a catastrophe could cost

rows.label: World population in the long run (people alive in a typical future year)

source.title: United Nations, Global Issues: Population (World Population Prospects 2024)
source.quote: After reaching this peak, it is expected to gradually decline to around 10.2 billion by the century's end.

rows.explainer: People alive in each future year, the yearly stream of healthy life a catastrophe that shrinks or ends humanity's future would cost: the UN's 2100 projection as the best guess (after its peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s). The range is ours: a lower population if decline continues past 2100, a higher one if it doesn't. Every model's future loss is this stream discounted at the shared rate (your discount rate is how much future generations count).

rows.label: Yearly chance of a pandemic as deadly as COVID-19

source.title: Duke Global Health Institute, Statistics say large pandemics are more likely than we thought (Marani, Katul, Pan and Parolari 2021, PNAS)
source.quote: It found the probability of a pandemic with similar impact to COVID-19 is about 2% in any year

rows.explainer: From four centuries of epidemic records, the yearly chance of a novel pandemic with COVID-19's intensity. The range is ours: half to twice the estimate, since the authors find new outbreaks becoming more frequent and the record is patchy. Read together with covid_excess_deaths, the size of the pandemic it describes.

rows.label: Deaths in a COVID-scale pandemic (WHO excess deaths, 2020-2021)

source.title: World Health Organization, 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021 (5 May 2022)
source.quote: between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2021 was approximately 14.9 million (range 13.3 million to 16.6 million)

rows.explainer: Deaths directly or indirectly caused by COVID-19 in its first two years: the size of the pandemic whose yearly chance is pandemic_probability_covid_scale. WHO's range.

rows.label: Share of new infectious diseases whose emergence land-use change drove (since 1960)

source.title: Future Earth, New IPBES report on escaping the pandemic era (IPBES Workshop Report on Biodiversity and Pandemics, 2020)
source.quote: The expansion of anthropogenic activities such as deforestation has caused the emergence of more than 30% of new diseases.

rows.explainer: IPBES's expert workshop: land-use change (deforestation, settlement in wild areas, expansion of crops and livestock) drove the emergence of more than 30% of new diseases reported since 1960. The range is ours: an expert synthesis, not a measured share.
